clue.text: Atonement from last character leaving Cornish town

indicators.note: leaving means the letter goes out of the town's name

parts.note: Penzance is a town in Cornwall, at the south-western tip of England
Z is the last letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone seeks forgiveness by moving away from a Cornish town.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'last character' is Z, the final letter of the alphabet; take it out of PENZANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Penance is self-punishment undertaken to make amends for wrongdoing, which is what atonement means.

clue.text: Birds greedily eat one's nuts

parts.note: to pig, or pig out, is to eat greedily

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of one's

explanation.surface: Birds gobble up somebody's nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like food for the birds, but it means crazy and rearranges ONES into EONS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigeons are common plump grey birds, often seen in towns and parks.

clue.text: Relative cutting fabric

parts.note: nan is an informal word for grandmother
keen can mean sharp, as a keen or cutting edge

explanation.surface: A family member snips a length of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting' looks like a verb acting on the fabric, but it is the adjective sharp.
explanation.definitionFit: Nankeen is a yellowish cotton cloth, originally made in Nanjing in China.

clue.text: Love hugging American boozers — ultimately, these might get hammered

indicators.note: hugging means the word wraps around the next letter

parts.note: love is a score of nil in tennis

indicators.note: ultimately means the last letter of the word that precedes it

parts.note: last letter of boozers

explanation.surface: Drinkers holding each other, who will end up drunk, or hammered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hammered' is slang for very drunk, which suits the boozers, but the definition means struck with a hammer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nails are driven into wood by striking them with a hammer.

clue.text: Lifts tops from one's torso and reveals bust

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters are rearranged
tops from means the first letter of each of the following words

parts.note: first letter of one's
first letter of torso
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone removes their tops and shows off their chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' and 'tops' look like clothing and the body, but bust means broken: rearrange O, T and REVEALS.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevators is the American word for lifts, the cars that carry people between floors.

clue.text: Lean and topple over part of aeroplane

parts.note: to cock something is to tilt it, to make it lean

indicators.note: over here means the word is turned back to front

parts.note: to tip is to topple

explanation.surface: An aircraft part tilts and falls over, as if describing a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lean' and 'topple' read like a plane going down, but to cock is to tilt, and 'over' turns the word for topple round.
explanation.definitionFit: The cockpit is the compartment at the front of a plane where the pilot sits.

clue.text: Lovely copper fastening

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a tie is something that fastens

explanation.surface: A beautiful copper clasp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lovely' looks like an adjective praising the clasp, but it is the noun for an attractive person.
explanation.definitionFit: A lovely is an attractive person, and a cutie is an informal word for the same.

clue.text: Craft or ancient vessel

indicators.note: to craft is to make or shape, so the letters are formed into a new word

explanation.surface: A choice between a boat and an old pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' and 'vessel' both look like boats, but craft is the verb signalling a rearrangement of OR ANCIENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A container is anything that holds something, which is a vessel in its broad sense.

clue.text: Left Charlie and Oscar under one colonnade

indicators.note: under means C and O come below I in this down answer

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
I is the Roman numeral one
C is Charlie in the NATO phonetic alphabet
O is Oscar in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Charlie and Oscar left together beneath a pillared walkway.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'under' means after, so C and O follow I.
explanation.definitionFit: A portico is a roofed porch supported by columns, a small colonnade at a building's entrance.

clue.text: Storm, it seems, oddly removed problem

indicators.note: oddly removed means the odd-numbered letters are taken away, leaving the even ones

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of it seems
a pest is a nuisance, a problem

explanation.surface: It appears a storm has strangely cleared away a difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of ITSEEMS leaves TEM.
explanation.definitionFit: A tempest is a violent windy storm, as in Shakespeare's play of that name.

clue.text: True information I included in French article

parts.note: gen is British slang for information

indicators.note: included in means the letter I goes inside the French word

parts.note: une is the French feminine indefinite article, 'a'

explanation.surface: A true fact gets slipped into a French newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper story, but it is the grammatical article UNE; GEN is British slang for information.
explanation.definitionFit: Something genuine is authentic and real, so a genuine account is a true one.

clue.text: Brown lead from the peculiar pet

parts.note: tan is a light brown colour

indicators.note: lead from means the opening letter of the word that follows

parts.note: first letter of the
rum is British slang for odd or peculiar

explanation.surface: A brown dog lead taken from a strange pet, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like an animal at the end of the surface, but here it is the old noun for a fit of sulking; 'rum' is British slang for strange.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet in the sense of a sulk or fit of bad temper is a tantrum, an outburst of childish anger.

clue.text: Exaggerate remaining condition

parts.note: over can mean left over, remaining
state means condition, as in a state of repair

explanation.surface: Someone overplays a lingering illness or situation.
explanation.definitionFit: To overstate is to claim more than is true, the same as to exaggerate or overclaim.

clue.text: Junior doctor possibly wants this result

definitions.meaning: junior doctors in Britain have campaigned for a pay rise
to ... is to result, as problems ... from a decision

explanation.walkthrough: The first part reads as two words, a rise in pay, which Britain's junior doctors have famously gone on strike for; the second is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To arise is to come about as a consequence, which is what to result means as a verb.

clue.text: Perhaps taste delicatessen's egg sandwiches

indicators.note: sandwiches means the phrase holds the answer between its outer letters

parts.note: the letters run across the end of delicatessen's and into egg

explanation.surface: A deli's egg sandwiches give a hint of their flavour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' looks like food from the deli, but it is a verb saying the phrase holds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Taste is one of the five senses, so it is an example of the answer, flagged by 'Perhaps'.

clue.text: The planes compromised those with trunks?

indicators.note: compromised means damaged, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Aircraft have been damaged; perhaps something was in their luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunks' looks like the luggage carried on the planes, but it means the long noses.
explanation.definitionFit: Elephants are the animals with a long flexible nose, called a trunk.

clue.text: Two dismissals in game? Perfect!

definitions.meaning: one batter out and then another, in cricket or baseball
... means complete, utter, as in an ... rogue

explanation.walkthrough: The first part reads literally as two outs, one after the other, which in cricket is two batters dismissed; the second is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Out-and-out means thorough or absolute, the sense of perfect in 'a perfect stranger'.

clue.text: Amazing chapter removed and editor's panic-stricken

indicators.note: removed means the letter is taken away

parts.note: terrific means amazing
ED is the abbreviation for editor; the 's stands for 'is', linking to the definition

explanation.surface: An editor panics after a brilliant chapter gets cut from the book.
explanation.walkthrough: TERRIFIC loses its final C, leaving TERRIFI, then ED is added.
explanation.definitionFit: To be terrified is to be extremely frightened, the same as panic-stricken.

clue.text: Academic reproofs us nastily, leaving university

indicators.note: nastily suggests the letters treated roughly into a new order
leaving means the named letter is taken out of the jumbled letters

parts.note: the fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A lecturer scolds us harshly as we leave the university.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one U from REPROOFSUS and rearrange the remaining nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A professor is a senior teacher at a university, the top rank of academic.

clue.text: Railway workers' drinks

definitions.meaning: the possessive is part of the surface
porter is a dark British beer

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe makes it read as the drinks belonging to the railway staff, but the two parts are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both station luggage carriers and glasses of a dark British ale brewed from roasted malt.

clue.text: Luxurious work uniform provided

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
lent means provided, as on loan

explanation.surface: A costly work uniform was given out.
explanation.definitionFit: Something opulent is rich and lavish, showing great wealth, which is what luxurious means.

clue.text: These could be vibrating in the wind, studies announced

definitions.text: These could be vibrating in the wind

indicators.note: announced means the word is spoken aloud and heard as another

parts.note: reads means studies, as one reads a subject at university

explanation.surface: Something trembles in a breeze while research findings are made public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The wind' suggests weather, but it is the wind section of an orchestra, where reeds vibrate in clarinets and oboes.
explanation.definitionFit: The reed in a clarinet or oboe is a thin strip that vibrates to make the sound of these woodwind instruments.

clue.text: Look at a cheeky girl wanting kiss in river

indicators.note: in means these letters go inside the river's name

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, in south-west England

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the letter is removed

parts.note: a minx is a cheeky or flirtatious girl
X is the sign for a kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Someone observes a cheeky girl who longs for a kiss while in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting' looks like desire for a kiss, but means lacking; the Exe is a river in Devon, England, and a minx is a cheeky girl.
explanation.definitionFit: To examine something is to inspect or study it closely, to look at it carefully.

clue.text: Decides former tennis player keeps dry

indicators.note: keeps means the name holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: Monica Seles is a former world number one tennis player
TT means teetotal, so dry, not drinking alcohol

explanation.surface: A retired tennis star chooses to stay off alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle a matter is to resolve or determine it, which is what decides means.

clue.text: Lousy, aggressive golf shot could land here

definitions.meaning: the long grass beside a golf fairway

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings of one word: unwell, violent, and the long grass off the fairway on a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers ill health, violent behaviour, and the unmown grass bordering a golf fairway.

clue.text: Wicked fish — it swallows a knight

parts.note: brill is a flatfish

indicators.note: swallows means the word takes the following letters inside it

parts.note: taken as written
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A villainous fish gulps down a knight, like a medieval tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' looks like evil, but it is the slang for excellent; IT swallows A and N, the chess knight.
explanation.definitionFit: Wicked is slang praise meaning excellent or great, the same informal sense as brilliant.

clue.text: By imbibing real ale regularly, this is what you get?

definitions.text: By imbibing real ale regularly, this is what you get?

indicators.note: imbibing means drinking in, so the word takes the letters inside it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter, here the second, fourth and sixth

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters of real ale

explanation.surface: A warning that steady beer drinking leads to a beer gut.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: drinking ale regularly gives you a paunch.
explanation.definitionFit: Habitual beer drinking is said to produce a large stomach, the so-called beer belly.

clue.text: Insinuating no rascal is telling tales

indicators.note: no means without, so these letters are removed

parts.note: implying means insinuating, suggesting indirectly
an imp is a mischievous child, a rascal

explanation.surface: A sneaky hint that a rogue is spreading gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: IMPLYING without IMP; 'telling tales' here means making things up.
explanation.definitionFit: Telling tales can mean telling untruths, which is what lying is.

clue.text: Endless bats enter area next to lake

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: L is a standard abbreviation for lake, as on maps

explanation.surface: An unending stream of bats flies into a region beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the animals, but it means crazy and signals rearranging ENTER into ETERN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something eternal has no beginning or end in time, so it lasts forever.

clue.text: Opening present — it is second dropped off by a student

parts.note: to be in is to be present, at home

indicators.note: dropped off means the letter is taken away from the end

parts.note: the two words written together
L is for learner, the student driver's L-plate

explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' and 'Opening' suggest unwrapping a gift; ITIS loses its S, and L is the learner plate.
explanation.definitionFit: An initial move is the first or opening one, as in the initial stages of a process.

clue.text: Please speak about female model making a comeback

indicators.note: about means the word goes around the reversed letters

parts.note: to say is to speak

indicators.note: making a comeback means these letters are read backwards

parts.note: to sit is to model, as an artist's model sits

explanation.surface: Someone talks about a female model returning to the catwalk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a comeback' sounds like a model's career revival, but it reverses the female-plus-model letters before they go inside the word for speak.
explanation.definitionFit: To satisfy someone is to give them what they want, so it means to please or gratify them.

clue.text: Some hairdresser giddily brought back stray

indicators.note: brought back means the letters are read in reverse
some means only part of the phrase is used

parts.note: the letters run across the end of hairdresser and the start of giddily

explanation.surface: A dizzy hairdresser returned a lost animal.
explanation.walkthrough: SSERGID sits across 'hairdresser giddily'; read it backwards. 'Stray' looks like a lost pet, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To digress is to wander off the main subject when speaking or writing, to stray from the point.
